title: The Sanctum Teachings · Episode 3
chapters: Entropy and the Arrow of Time

units.t: The Sanctum Teachings. Episode three.
In this episode: Entropy and the Arrow of Time, The Fermi Paradox, The Replication Crisis and Why Complex Societies Collapse.
Part one. Entropy and the Arrow of Time.
Almost every law of physics works just as well backwards, yet eggs never unscramble.
The reason is one modest law with cosmic consequences, and it may explain why you remember yesterday but not tomorrow.
The glass that never unshatters.
A wine glass slips and shatters.
Play the film backwards and anyone can tell something is wrong: shards do not leap up and fuse.
Yet the laws governing those shards, from Newton's mechanics to electromagnetism and, to an excellent approximation, quantum theory, work equally well in reverse.
Nothing in the equations says which way time should flow.
The one-way world of ageing, cooling coffee and memory comes from the second law of thermodynamics.
It began with steam engines.
In the early nineteenth century, Sadi Carnot asked how much work could be squeezed from heat.
Heat flows by itself from hot to cold, never the reverse, and every real engine wastes some energy.
In 1865 Rudolf Clausius named this pattern entropy.
In an isolated system it stays the same or rises, and a spontaneous fall is never observed.
Counting the arrangements.
Toss one hundred coins.
There is one way to get all heads, but roughly 10^29 ways to get fifty of each.
In the 1870s Ludwig Boltzmann saw that this is what entropy is.
A macrostate is what you can see, such as a gas's temperature and pressure.
A microstate is the exact position and speed of every molecule.
Entropy counts the microstates that fit a macrostate: S = k log W, the formula carved on his tombstone in Vienna.
So the second law is statistical.
Pour milk into coffee and it swirls to beige.
Nothing forbids it from unmixing, but mixed arrangements outnumber separated ones so hugely that you would wait far longer than the age of the universe.
That drift towards the most arrangements is the arrow of time.
The past hypothesis.
There is a catch in Boltzmann's logic.
Statistics is symmetric in time, so the same reasoning predicts that the past had higher entropy than now.
The way out is an extra assumption, which the philosopher David Albert called the past hypothesis: the universe began in an astonishingly low-entropy state.
That sounds odd, because the early universe was a hot, almost perfectly smooth gas, which looks maximally disordered.
But gravity flips the intuition.
For gravitating matter, smoothness is the special, low-entropy state, and clumping into stars, galaxies and black holes raises entropy.
Many physicists link our sense of cause and effect, and the fact that we remember the past but not the future, to this rising tide.
Every broken glass and fading memory borrows its direction from that special beginning.
Why the Big Bang was so special remains an open question.
Maxwell's demon.
In 1867 the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell imagined a box of gas split by a wall with a tiny trapdoor.
Beside it sits a minute being, later nicknamed a demon, watching each molecule approach.
It lets fast molecules from the left through, and slow ones from the right.
Over time, one side grows hot and the other cold.
The demon seems to have created order and a usable temperature difference without doing any work, flatly contradicting the second law.
For decades the puzzle resisted a satisfying answer.
It hinted that something essential was missing from physics: the role of knowledge itself.
Information has a price.
The resolution took about a century.
In 1929 Leo Szilard linked the demon's knowledge of molecules to entropy.
In 1961 Rolf Landauer at IBM showed that erasing one bit of information must release a minimum amount of heat, proportional to temperature.
In 1982 Charles Bennett completed the argument: the demon's memory fills up, and wiping it to keep working generates at least as much entropy as the sorting removed.
The second law survives.
In 2012, experiments measured heat release close to Landauer's limit when a single bit was erased.
The lesson is profound: information is physical, and forgetting costs energy.
Entropy links steam engines, computers, memory and the birth of the cosmos into one idea about counting possibilities.
The key idea: The basic laws of physics barely distinguish past from future, and entropy is what gives everyday life its one-way direction.
Part two. The Fermi Paradox.
The galaxy is old, vast and full of planets, so where is everybody?
A question tossed out over lunch in 1950 has become one of the most unsettling puzzles about our own future.
Where is everybody.

At a lunch table at Los Alamos in the summer of 1950, the physicist Enrico Fermi, already famous for building the first nuclear reactor, was chatting with Edward Teller, Herbert York and Emil Konopinski about flying saucer reports.
According to later recollections, he suddenly asked something like "Where is everybody?"
Accounts differ on his exact words.
The logic is about time.
The Milky Way is about a hundred thousand light years across, and many of its stars are billions of years older than the Sun.

Calculations popularised by Michael Hart in 1975 suggest probes at a modest fraction of light speed could spread across it in a few million to tens of millions of years, a blink against a galaxy over ten billion years old.
One expansionist civilisation would be enough.
Yet we see no visitors, probes or signals.
Drake's equation.
In 1961 the radio astronomer Frank Drake wrote an agenda for a meeting at Green Bank, West Virginia, in the form of an equation.
It multiplies factors such as star formation, planets, habitable worlds, the chance life begins and becomes intelligent, and how long civilisations keep broadcasting.
It was never a precise calculator.
It turned a vague question into specific unknowns.
Thanks to missions like NASA's Kepler, we now know planets are abundant.
The trouble lies further along: we have one example each of life, intelligence and technology, all of them us.
Answers range from millions of civilisations to far fewer than one.
A 2018 analysis by Sandberg, Drexler and Ord argued that, with uncertainty treated honestly, there is a substantial chance we are alone in the galaxy.
The Great Filter.
In the late 1990s the economist Robin Hanson offered a sobering framework.

Picture the path from lifeless chemistry to a star-spanning civilisation as steps: self-replicating molecules, simple cells, complex cells, multicellular life, intelligence, technology and expansion into space.
Since the galaxy appears empty, at least one step must be extraordinarily improbable.
Hanson called it the Great Filter.
The crucial question is where it lies.
If it is behind us, perhaps at the origin of life or the leap to complex cells, we are a rare fluke that has passed the hardest test.
If it lies ahead, almost every civilisation at our stage fails before spreading outward, and our prospects look grim.
Rare, quiet, early or gone.
Proposed answers fall into four broad families.

The rare Earth view, argued by Peter Ward and Donald Brownlee in 2000, holds that simple life may be common but complex life needs a long run of lucky conditions, such as a stable star, plate tectonics and a large moon.
Second, they are out there but quiet: perhaps advanced civilisations deliberately avoid contact, communicate in ways we cannot detect, or find expansion pointless.
Third, we are simply early, among the first in a universe that is still young in cosmic terms.
The darkest family proposes self-destruction: civilisations that master powerful technology tend to destroy themselves through war, environmental collapse or something we have not yet imagined.
Each idea is coherent, and none is yet supported by direct evidence.
What the silence means.
Here is the twist.
In 2008 the philosopher Nick Bostrom wrote that he hoped searches for life on Mars would find nothing.
If life arose independently on Mars, the origin of life is probably easy.
That makes it less likely that the Great Filter is behind us, and more likely that it lies ahead.
Not every scientist accepts this logic, but it shows how the paradox reaches back towards us.
It is also worth remembering how little we have looked.
One 2018 estimate compared the search so far to examining a hot tub's worth of water from all of Earth's oceans.
The silence may mean nothing yet.
But if it does mean something, the safest response is the same either way: take our long-term survival seriously.
The key idea: If technological civilisations were common, even slow expansion should have filled the galaxy long ago, yet we see no sign of them.
Part three. The Replication Crisis.
Scientists using standard methods once 'proved' people could sense the future.
Understanding how that happened will change how you read every headline that begins 'A new study shows'.
When methods proved the impossible.
In 2011 the Cornell psychologist Daryl Bem published a paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
Across nine experiments involving about a thousand participants, he reported evidence that people could be influenced by events that had not yet happened.
In plain terms, it suggested precognition.
Most scientists did not believe it, and attempts to repeat the experiments generally failed.
The deeper shock was that Bem had used the ordinary statistical tools and research practices of his field, and the paper had passed peer review.
If standard methods could produce convincing evidence for something almost certainly false, how many other published findings were equally hollow?
The question helped ignite what is now called the replication crisis, a reckoning that has spread well beyond psychology.
What a p-value says.
Most studies hinge on a number called the p-value.
Suppose you test whether a new drug lowers blood pressure.
The p-value answers a narrow question: if the drug truly did nothing, how often would chance alone produce results at least as striking as these?
By a convention popularised by the statistician Ronald Fisher, results with p below 0.
05 are called statistically significant.
Crucially, a p-value is not the probability that the finding is true, nor the probability that it was a fluke.
And significant does not mean important: with a large enough sample, a trivially small effect can clear the bar.
In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued an unusual formal statement warning against these misreadings, which are common even among working researchers.
How false positives get published.
When there is no effect, about one test in twenty looks significant at the 0.
05 threshold.
Now imagine a researcher who can choose which outcomes to report, which outliers to exclude, or when to stop collecting data.
Each choice is another chance at a lucky result.
This is p-hacking.
In 2011 Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn showed such flexibility could push false positives far above five per cent, even "finding" that a Beatles song made people younger.
Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken named a subtler version, the garden of forking paths: honest researchers deciding after seeing the data can fool themselves.
Then comes publication bias.
If twenty labs test a useless idea, one gets a significant result and publishes it.
The other nineteen sit in a "file drawer", as Robert Rosenthal put it in 1979.
Testing the record.
In 2005 the physician John Ioannidis published "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False".
His argument was mathematical: when studies are small, effects modest, hypotheses long shots and researchers flexible, false positives can outnumber true ones.
Later analyses disputed how high the rate is in some fields, but the warning endured.
Direct tests followed.
The Open Science Collaboration, about 270 researchers coordinated by Brian Nosek, repeated one hundred studies published in 2008 in three prominent psychology journals.
Results, published in Science in 2015, were sobering.
Nearly all the originals had been significant, but only about 36 per cent of the replications were, with effects roughly half the size.
This did not prove every failed study wrong, since one replication can itself miss a real effect.
Fixing science, reading wisely.
Science has begun to repair itself.
In pre-registration, researchers publicly record their hypotheses and analysis plan before collecting data, closing off the garden of forking paths.
In registered reports, journals agree to publish a study based on its design, before results are known, which defeats the file drawer.
Larger samples, shared data and multi-lab replications are increasingly common.
As a reader, you can apply the same discipline.
Be wary of a single study, especially a small one with a surprising, headline-friendly result and a p-value just under 0.
Ask whether the finding has been independently replicated, whether the effect is large enough to matter, and whether the study was pre-registered.
Treat science as a slowly converging conversation, not a stream of final verdicts, and you will rarely be fooled.
The key idea: A respected psychologist used standard methods to find evidence of precognition, which exposed a problem with the methods themselves.
Part four. Why Complex Societies Collapse.
Empires that seemed eternal have unravelled within a few generations.
One bold theory says the very complexity that makes societies strong can quietly become the thing that breaks them.
A slow unravelling.
In 476 a Germanic general, Odoacer, deposed a teenage emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and did not bother to appoint a replacement.
Textbooks mark this as the fall of the Western Roman Empire, yet it was barely a headline.
The real story was a slow unravelling: frontiers breached, provinces lost, taxes shrinking, cities emptying.
The Eastern Empire survived until 1453.
In his 1988 book The Collapse of Complex Societies, the anthropologist Joseph Tainter argued that societies solve problems by adding complexity: more officials, soldiers, rules and infrastructure.
Early investments pay handsomely, but each extra layer delivers less than the last.
Eventually a society spends ever more just to maintain itself, leaving little reserve for shocks.
Collapse, a rapid loss of complexity, can then be a rational response, as people find they are better off without a burdensome centre.
Rome through Tainter's eyes.
Early conquests were hugely profitable for Rome, bringing plunder and taxable provinces.
Once expansion stopped, the empire had to fund long frontiers from its own resources.
During the crises of the third century, emperors repeatedly debased the silver coinage, cutting its silver content, which fed inflation.
Reforms under Diocletian and later emperors enlarged the army and the bureaucracy, and the tax burden grew heavier.
On Tainter's reading, many farmers in the west found that the costs of empire outweighed its protections.
Some land went out of cultivation, and some people even welcomed or tolerated new rulers.
Each emergency was met with more complexity, until the western provinces could no longer sustain the system that was supposed to protect them.
Decline or transformation.
Not every historian accepts the language of collapse.
Scholars of late antiquity, influenced by Peter Brown, stress continuity and creativity after 400: the spread of Christianity, new art, and new kingdoms that often kept Roman law and administration.
In this view the empire was transformed rather than destroyed.
Others push back.

The historian Bryan Ward-Perkins, in a 2005 book, pointed to material evidence of a striking fall in living standards in parts of the west: cruder pottery, fewer coins, smaller buildings, and in some regions even smaller cattle.
Both views capture something real.
Elite culture and religion adapted and flourished in new forms, while for many ordinary people the material world became poorer, simpler and more local.
The Bronze Age collapse.
Over three thousand years ago the eastern Mediterranean was remarkably connected.
Egyptian pharaohs, Hittite kings, Mycenaean palaces, the merchant city of Ugarit and Cyprus's copper producers traded letters, diplomats and goods.
A shipwreck off Uluburun in Turkey carried copper, tin, glass and luxuries from many lands.
Then, between about 1200 and 1150 BC, much of this system disintegrated.
The Hittite capital Hattusa was abandoned, Ugarit was destroyed, and most Mycenaean palaces were burned or deserted.
Linear B writing vanished from Greece, and a poorer, less literate "dark age" followed.
Egypt survived, but weakened.
Egyptian inscriptions blame seaborne raiders called the Sea Peoples, who may have been a symptom as much as a cause.
Researchers also cite drought, earthquakes, famine, revolts and disrupted trade.
Eric Cline argued for a systems collapse: several stresses hitting a tightly linked network, so failures cascaded.
Diamond and the lessons.

In his 2005 book Collapse, the geographer Jared Diamond proposed five factors: environmental damage, climate change, hostile neighbours, loss of friendly trading partners and, most important, how a society responds to its problems.
He used cases such as the Norse settlements in Greenland to argue that collapse reflects choices as well as fate.
Critics, in the 2010 volume Questioning Collapse, argued that he underplayed resilience and that cases like Easter Island are more complicated.
Still, the debates share useful lessons.
Tightly linked systems can transmit shocks quickly.
Spending more just to keep existing systems running can quietly erode resilience.
And societies that recognise slow threats early, and keep the capacity to adapt, have the best chance of transforming rather than breaking.
The key idea: Rome's western empire faded over generations, and Tainter argued societies collapse when added complexity yields diminishing returns.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is the one-way direction of everyday events puzzling to physicists?
Answer. The basic laws work almost equally well in reverse.
Question two. Why does the age of the galaxy sharpen the Fermi paradox?
Answer. Slow colonisation could fill it in a fraction of its age.
Question three. Why did Bem's 2011 precognition paper alarm many scientists?
Answer. Ordinary methods supported a claim almost certainly false.
Question four. According to Joseph Tainter, why do complex societies collapse?
Answer. Added complexity eventually yields diminishing returns.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
